header: IN THE HIGH COURT OF SINDH, CIRCUIT COURT, MIRPURKHAS
Respondents No.1 to 3 : The State through Mr. Neel Parkash
Respondent No.4 Khushal Das s/o Damro Mal
body: ZULFIQAR ALI SANGI. J:- Through the instant criminal misc: application, the applicants have called in question the order dated 11.11.2025 passed by the learned Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, Umerkot, in Criminal Miscellaneous Application No.1312 of 2025, whereby the application filed by respondent No.4, Khushal Das, under Sections 22-A and 22-B Cr.P.C. was allowed and the SHO, Police Station Umerkot City, was directed to record his statement under Section 154 Cr.P.C and, if the same disclosed commission of a cognizable offence, to register an FIR and proceed with the investigation in accordance with law.

2. Learned counsel for the applicants contends that the impugned order has been passed without proper consideration of the material available on record and the police report, which disclosed a longstanding dispute between the parties concerning landed property situated in Deh Vehro Thar, Taluka and District Umerkot. He submits that the parties have been involved in previous litigation regarding the disputed property and that the present application is nothing but a counterblast to FIR No.195 of 2025, registered against respondent No.4 on 26.10.2025, at the instance of one Abdul Sattar Unar. He further contends that respondent No.4, after submitting an application before the SSP, Umerkot, on 03.11.2025, subsequently approached the learned Justice of Peace by levelling false and exaggerated allegations of house trespass, assault and robbery, without producing any medical evidence or independent corroboration. According to him, the learned Justice of Peace failed to examine the relevant circumstances and the police report and passed the impugned order in a mechanical manner, without recording proper reasons. He, therefore, prays that the impugned order may be set aside.

3. Conversely, learned counsel for respondent No.4 supports the impugned order and submits that the allegations contained in the application prima facie disclose commission of cognizable offences, including house trespass, criminal intimidation, assault and robbery. He contends that the existence of a previous property dispute between the parties does not, by itself, furnish lawful justification for the police to refuse registration of an FIR where the information discloses a cognizable offence. He, therefore, prays for dismissal of the instant revision application.

4. Learned Deputy Prosecutor General, appearing for the State, has placed reliance upon the police report and submits that the parties are involved in longstanding hostility and litigation over the disputed property, whereas the police, upon preliminary inquiry, found the allegations to be exaggerated and could not verify the alleged occurrence.
5. I have heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the available record with their assistance.

6. The controversy requiring determination is whether, in the peculiar circumstances of the case, the learned Ex-Officio Justice of Peace was justified in allowing the application under Sections 22-A and 22-B Cr.P.C. without adequately examining the material circumstances reflected in the police report and the previous litigation between the parties. It is settled that the jurisdiction exercised by an Ex-Officio Justice of Peace under Section 22-A(6) Cr.P.C. is intended to ensure that the police discharge their statutory obligations in accordance with law. At the same time, such jurisdiction is not to be exercised mechanically or as a matter of course. The learned Justice of Peace is required to apply judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of each case and determine whether the information placed before him, when considered in its entirety, prima facie discloses commission of a cognizable offence. The principles laid down by the Honourable Supreme Court in Syed Qamber Ali Shah v. Province of Sindh (2024 SCMR 1123) also require that the jurisdiction of the Justice of Peace be exercised within its prescribed legal limits and without undertaking an adjudication of the merits of the proposed criminal case.

7. In the present case, the record reflects that the parties are embroiled in a longstanding dispute concerning landed property measuring approximately two acres situated in Survey No.10, Deh Vehro Thar, Taluka and District Umerkot. It further appears that proceedings between the parties have previously been initiated before different forums, including proceedings relating to the alleged illegal dispossession of the disputed property. The applicants have also placed on record the fact that respondent No.4 was nominated in FIR No.195 of 2025, registered on 26.10.2025, and that the present allegations relate to an occurrence allegedly taking place on the same date. These circumstances, particularly the background of previous litigation and the timing of the allegations, were relevant considerations requiring due examination by the learned Justice of Peace. It is correct that the existence of a civil or property dispute does not automatically exclude the possibility of commission of a cognizable offence, nor can the police refuse registration of an FIR merely on the basis of a preliminary opinion regarding the truthfulness of the allegations. However, equally, the jurisdiction under Section 22- A(6) Cr.P.C. cannot be exercised without an objective assessment of the material placed before the Court. The police report, previous proceedings between the parties and the circumstances surrounding the alleged occurrence were relevant aspects of the controversy. The learned Justice of Peace, while noticing the existence of such dispute and previous litigation, proceeded to draw conclusions regarding the conduct of the parties and the alleged misuse of legal process without recording any cogent reasons supported by the material available on record.

8. It is also significant that the impugned order does not adequately address the objections raised by the proposed accused, particularly those concerning the previous litigation, the registration of FIR No.195 of 2025 and the circumstances in which the subsequent allegations were levelled. Although the learned Justice of Peace was not required to conduct a detailed trial or determine the veracity of the allegations, he was nevertheless required to pass a speaking order demonstrating proper application of judicial mind to the material placed before him. The impugned order, to this extent, suffers from material irregularity and non-consideration of relevant circumstances, thereby warranting interference by this Court.

9. It is noteworthy that the respondent has failed to place on record any medical evidence whatsoever to substantiate the alleged injuries purportedly sustained at the time of the incident. Despite having been afforded an opportunity by this Court, learned counsel for the respondent has remained unable to produce any medical certificate, medico-legal report, treatment record or other corroborative material in support of such allegation. It is a wellsettled principle of law that a party asserting a particular fact bears the burden of proving the same through cogent and reliable evidence. Mere assertion, unsupported by any independent or documentary corroboration, cannot be treated as proof of the alleged fact. Consequently, in the absence of any medical evidence, the allegation of injuries remains unsubstantiated and cannot be relied upon as an established circumstance.

10. For the foregoing reasons, the instant criminal misc: application is allowed. Consequently, the impugned order dated 11.11.2025 passed by the learned Sessions Judge/Ex-Officio Justice of Peace, Umerkot, in Criminal Miscellaneous Application No.1312 of 2025 is hereby set aside.
11. The instant criminal misc. application stands disposed of in the above terms.
